transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-05 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Nina Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Mendez (Redwood SE), Ava Thompson (CTO, LakeStream), Jon Park (Platform), Maya Singh (ML)

Summary (auto):
Quick discovery focused on latency/throughput targets, evaluation between Hosted/Dedicated/Private, and a plan for a 48h dedicated pilot. Customer cares about p95 under interactive latency, concurrency for live captioning use-case, streaming token/sec, and data residency/SOC2.

[00:00] Nina: All right, hey everyone thanks for taking the time, um this is Nina from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, with me is Carlos our solutions engineer. Can you do quick intros from LakeStream?

[00:12] Ava: Yeah hi I'm Ava, CTO at LakeStream. We run a live captioning and highlights product for streaming platforms. We're evaluating inferencing for on-demand transcripts and a low-latency assistant for editors.

[00:24] Jon: Jon, platform engineer, I'll own the hookup and VPC/network side.

[00:28] Maya: Maya, I lead ML, mainly model selection, latency budgets, and quality gating.

[00:35] Nina: Great thanks. Our agenda is to understand your p95/time-to-first-token goals, concurrency expectations, how streaming is used (token/sec), and any security/regulatory constraints for data residency. Then we'll map Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private options.

[00:50] Carlos: Quick note: we'll also want a sample workload and a few prompt sets to run a realistic token/sec profile. The benchmark we recommend tries to mimic live streaming with prefix cache and partial outputs.

[01:05] Ava: High level targets: for editor assistant flows we want p95 under 800ms for responses up to 256 tokens. For live captioning (streaming) we want steady-state token emit at 40 tokens/sec per stream and a p95 for first token under 300ms ideally. Overall concurrency: 150 concurrently active editor sessions, and up to 400 concurrent low-priority captioning streams. Does that map to how you think about it?

[01:36] Carlos: Yeah that's a helpful start. Two clarifications: when you say p95 under 800ms for 256 tokens, is that end-to-end or just server-side generation? Network and client-side jitter will add overhead. Also for streaming, is 40 tps sustained or bursty?

[01:50] Ava: Good point. Targets are server-side generation p95. Network budget is separate but we expect Redwood's SLO to be measured at your API edge. The 40 tps is typical sustained for captioning segments, bursts can go up to 120 tps for a few seconds.

[02:06] Nina: Noted. Let's talk topology decisions: Hosted gives fastest time-to-value, Dedicated gives predictable throughput and capacity isolation (we can reserve GPU pools to hit your concurrency targets), Private (VPC/on-prem) is for strict data residency and KMS/HSM control. Any legal or residency hard constraints?

[02:28] Maya: We need EU data residency for EU viewers and SOC2 compliance for the enterprise customers. Private deployment is attractive for some accounts but we want to compare cost first. Also SSO via SAML and audit logs are must-haves.

[02:42] Carlos: All supported. Hosted can be configured with region pinning and enterprise plans include retention and audit logs. Private gives full customer-managed network and KMS integration. For the bench we'll show both Hosted and a Dedicated config with identical model variants to compare p95 and cost.

[03:02] Jon: On network specifics: we have interconnect into GCP eu-west1 and a private peering to our CDN. If we go Private we'll want to run in our VPC and use their ENIs, firewall rules, etc. Can you support that?

[03:16] Carlos: Yep, our Private agent supports VPC peering, we can provide a checklist. Some customers also place a dedicated egress for consistent latency.

[03:25] Ava: Okay let's talk numbers. For editor assistant: 150 concurrent sessions, average request size 60 input tokens, expect 200 output tokens at 25 tokens/sec emission. For captioning: 400 concurrent streams with 40 tps emission but smaller model context. How do you size GPUs and batch settings?

[03:46] Carlos: Roughly speaking, for autoregressive models, peak GPU utilization depends on batch size, sequence length and quantization. For a 200-token gen at 25 tps, you can often hit P95 under 800ms with an M60-like dedicated cluster (note: we used shorthand) using continuous batching and prefix caching. But we typically recommend a Dedicated cluster with autoscale for your concurrency and also enabling prefix/KV cache for editors since many prompts share prefixes. For captioning we might favor a lighter model or trimmed context to hit the first-token p95 target.

[04:20] Maya: When you say continuous batching, is there an added latency penalty for waiting to form batches? We need per-chat low tail latency.

[04:28] Carlos: Good question. Our runtime does workload-aware batching: it respects per-route latency SLOs and uses dynamic batch windows. For strict p95, we can set batch windows to low ms ranges so you get little batching delay but that increases GPU cost. That's the tradeoff — latency vs unit cost. We usually show 3 configs: latency-optimized, balanced, and cost-optimized with different batch windows and quantization.

[04:54] Jon: What about KV cache for chat? If editors are doing follow-ups, a warm KV cache would help reduce compute for subsequent tokens, right?

[05:02] Carlos: Exactly, KV cache avoids recomputing earlier attention. For conversational sessions we hold per-session KV cache in memory; this reduces per-token latency and GPU work. We can also do prefix caching at the route level to reuse common system and prompt prefixes across sessions. We'll include expected token/sec and cost delta with KV enabled vs disabled in the sizing sheet.

[05:23] Ava: We have some heavy multimodal short transcripts that force longer context windows occasionally. How much does sequence length variability spike p95?

[05:33] Carlos: Sequence length variability can cause head-of-line issues: long contexts occupy the GPU longer. Smart routing helps: we can route long-context heavy requests to different instance types or fallback to lower-priority capacity to avoid impacting short low-latency requests. We'll show an example policy where editor assistant traffic is pinned to low-latency nodes and long batch jobs go to burst or cheaper nodes.

[05:57] Maya: Any notes on quantization and quality regressions? We don't want hallucinations to spike after quantizing.

[06:05] Carlos: We recommend quantization profiles per model: int8 for many workloads is fine, but we do per-prompt evals and quality monitoring. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles and run regressions against your prompt set. We also include rollbacks and A/B testing so we don't silently degrade.

[06:22] Ava: Good. For streaming captioning, first-token p95 300ms is ambitious. Can you show an architecture to get there?

[06:31] Carlos: For first-token p95 under 300ms, typical design is: colocate a small specialized shallow model for immediate token generation (fast), and asynchronously call a larger model for higher-quality re-ranks or expansions. Alternatively, run a very low-latency instance class (e.g., smaller sequence-optimized kernels) reserved for captioning with minimal batching. That is more expensive.

[06:54] Jon: Network jitter when TCP traverses our CDN occasionally adds 80-120ms; so we need server-side targets to be even tighter.

[07:02] Nina: We'll show network margin assumptions. In sizing we'll present server-side p95 targets that account for expected network delta and suggest edge co-location where needed.

[07:12] Ava: How do we validate p95 in your benchmarks? Is it token-to-token or response completion?

[07:18] Carlos: We produce both metrics: time-to-first-token (TTFT), and time-to-last-token (TTLT) per response, and we report p50/p95/p99 for both. For streaming we focus on TTFT and token emission rate stability. We can instrument synthetic clients that mimic your load shape - and we'll ask you for the 24h traffic window so we can replay realistic burst patterns.

[07:40] Maya: Are there prebuilt scripts? We prefer not to re-implement load drivers.

[07:44] Carlos: Yes, we'll provide our benchmark repo (shell+python) with examples for streaming via websockets and batch via REST. We can parameterize tokens/sec, concurrent sessions, and burst windows.

[07:55] Jon: For Dedicated, what are typical autoscale behaviors? For example, how long to provision more GPU nodes under a spike?

[08:03] Carlos: Autoscale is based on target utilization and queue depth. Cold provisioning of new GPU nodes can be 2-6 minutes depending on infra. For immediate spikes we recommend reserved burst capacity or hybrid model where a warm pool handles spikes. We can also use fallback to hosted spare capacity if you purchase the enterprise plan.

[08:20] Ava: Pricing sensitivity: our finance team will push back on big reserved clusters. Can you show cost tradeoffs?

[08:27] Nina: Absolutely — we'll include cost-per-1000-tokens for different configs: Hosted balanced, Dedicated small committed + burst, and Private with customer infra. Dedicated has predictable monthly commit but lower per-token when fully utilized; Hosted is pay-as-you-go but unit cost can be higher at scale. We'll include a modeled 6-month TCO.

[08:47] Maya: Security question: for Private, is there an audit trail and KMS/HSM integration? We need forensic logs and separation of keys per account.

[08:55] Carlos: Yes. Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations, and audit logs with exportable event streams. We also support SAML SSO, RBAC, and per-token lineage for compliance. We'll attach our SOC2 docs and the Private deployment checklist in the follow-up.

[09:12] Ava: Great. Any known gotchas when migrating a prototype from Hosted to Private?

[09:18] Carlos: Usually it's network config and egress. Also model artifacts need to be staged for Private image builds — we assist with that. Deployment patterns are the same; the API surface remains identical so application changes are minimal. The main friction is provisioning and security approvals on your side.

[09:33] Nina: Let's sketch the pilot: we propose a 48-hour Dedicated pilot where we reserve a cluster sized for your 150 concurrent editor sessions and 400 caption streams low-priority. We'll run replay against the 24h traffic window, instrument p50/p95/p99, provide kernel-level tracing, and a cost report. Does that sound useful?

[09:53] Ava: Yes, that gives us the data we need. Timeline wise we want results before our Q4 architecture sync end of month. Can you do the pilot next week?

[10:03] Nina: We can tentatively schedule pilot start 2026-11-10 pending paperwork. Carlos will scope exact GPU counts once you share the traffic dump.

[10:11] Carlos: I'll also include two configurations for the pilot: latency-optimized (lower batching, reserved nodes) and cost-balanced (higher batching, quantization). We'll capture both configs' p95 and token throughput.

[10:22] Jon: For the benchmark data we'll need access to telemetry and metrics. Will you provide guidance on which metrics to collect from our side?

[10:28] Carlos: Yes, we'll provide a metrics checklist: API latencies (TTFT/TTLT), per-token throughput, GPU utilization, queue depth, KV cache hit rates, and network egress RTTs.

[10:40] Maya: On the sample prompt set, we have three major flows: quick edit assistant, long-form summarization, and streaming captions. We'll prepare 200 prompts per flow.

[10:50] Ava: Also, can you include a fallback policy for model outages? We want graceful degradation, like falling back to a smaller model or cached responses.

[10:58] Carlos: Absolutely. Redwood supports automatic fallback to compatible model variants and region fallback. We'll show a canary policy and an automatic rollback strategy in the rollout plan.

[11:10] Nina: Any questions on cost controls? We offer token-level budgets, hard quotas and per-route rate limiting.

[11:16] Jon: We'll need per-team budgets and alerts. Also show per-route perf by token.

[11:21] Carlos: Covered — Console provides token-level breakdown and per-route latency.

[11:27] (brief cross-talk)

[11:29] Ava: Okay let's recap next steps verbally.

[11:31] Nina: Recap: 1) Nina sends sizing spreadsheet + pricing by tomorrow. 2) LakeStream to send sample prompts and a 24h traffic dump by 2026-11-08. 3) Carlos provides benchmark scripts and two pilot config suggestions by 2026-11-09. 4) Agree pilot start date (tentatively 2026-11-10).

[11:52] Maya: That aligns. Any blockers from Redwood side?

[11:55] Carlos: Nothing blocking. We'll also include SOC2 & Private deployment checklist in the follow-up.

[11:59] Nina: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow-up with calendar invite for the pilot kickoff and share artifacts.

[12:05] Ava: Thanks y'all.

(End of call)
